oneSentence: An adversarial attack is a deliberate attempt to exploit an AI system so it fails or produces an attacker-chosen result.
plainExplanation:
An adversarial attack is a deliberate attempt to exploit a weakness in an AI system so it produces a failure that benefits the attacker. The term is broad. It does not by itself identify when the attack happens or which mechanism it uses.

A common form is an input-time evasion attack. The attacker crafts an image, sound clip or other input so the model produces an incorrect or attacker-chosen result during use. The crafted input may look ordinary to a person, but subtle changes are not required.

An adversarial example is one crafted input used to trigger such a failure. The attack is the wider method or attempt. Data poisoning specifically changes training or update data. Prompt injection specifically uses malicious instructions in text to override an assistant’s intended rules.

The input-time examples on this page illustrate evasion attacks. Their goal may be misclassification, bypass of a safeguard or another chosen result. They do not represent every kind of adversarial attack.

everydayAnalogy.title: A delivery check fooled by a manipulated manifest
everydayAnalogy.story: At a warehouse, a clerk checks whether a shipping manifest matches the boxes on a pallet before release. A dishonest sender keeps the goods the same but edits the manifest so key codes look valid at a glance and the checking procedure passes the pallet. The clerk follows the usual process and releases it, even though the paperwork was crafted to trigger the wrong result. Nothing was physically forced open; the weakness was in how the checking system reacted to the input it was given.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A human clerk can pause, ask questions and use common sense in ways many models cannot. In real adversarial machine learning, very small mathematical changes can matter even when people do not notice them, especially for images and audio. For language models, the attack may involve instructions hidden in text rather than document formatting tricks alone. So the warehouse story helps with the idea of input manipulation, but it does not capture the full technical behaviour of models.

visual.title: How an adversarial attack changes an AI system’s output
visual.learningObjective: After viewing, the reader should be able to explain that the attacker alters the input at use time so the same model produces a different, harmful or incorrect result.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow diagram with two lanes. The top lane shows a normal input passing through a model to a normal output. The bottom lane shows a similar-looking but crafted input passing through the same model to a wrong or unsafe output. Read from left to right, then compare the two lanes.

steps.label: Normal input
steps.explanation: Show an ordinary input that the system is expected to handle, such as a photo, document or prompt.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a rectangle labelled 'normal input' on the top left with small neutral icons for image, text and audio beneath it.

steps.label: Same model
steps.explanation: Both lanes use the same model and settings; the system itself has not visibly changed.
steps.visualInstruction: Place one central rounded box labelled 'model' spanning both lanes, with arrows from each input lane into it.

steps.label: Expected output
steps.explanation: With the ordinary input, the model produces the intended result, such as a correct label or a safe response.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a top-right rectangle labelled 'expected output' with a green border and an arrow from the model.

steps.label: Crafted input
steps.explanation: An attacker makes a subtle or strategic change to the input so it still appears acceptable or plausible.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a bottom-left rectangle labelled 'crafted input' with a small highlight mark showing altered text or pixels, but keep it visually similar to the normal input.

steps.label: Failure at use time
steps.explanation: The crafted input causes the model to misclassify, ignore a guardrail or produce another attacker-chosen result.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a bottom-right rectangle labelled 'wrong or unsafe output' with an amber border and arrow from the model; add a side note: 'attack via input, not necessarily system break-in'.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap each lane to highlight its path and reveal a short caption: 'normal processing' or 'adversarial path'.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This diagram compares two paths through the same AI model. In the top path, a normal input enters the model and the output is the expected one. In the bottom path, a crafted input that looks similar enters that same model, but the output becomes wrong or unsafe. The point is causal: the attacker changes the input at use time, not necessarily the software or hardware, and that change is enough to alter the result.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static two-lane comparison is shown with no animation. The top lane reads normal input, model, expected output. The bottom lane reads crafted input, same model, wrong or unsafe output. A note states that the attack works by manipulating input rather than necessarily breaking into the system.

workedExample.scenario: A building entrance uses an image model to read printed visitor badges and match the badge type to an allowed access list.
workedExample.input: Normal badge text: 'VISITOR - CONFERENCE'. Crafted badge includes extra printed patterning around the text that looks decorative to staff but changes how the model reads it.
process: The system is trained to classify badge images into categories such as visitor, contractor and staff.
A normal printed badge is photographed by the camera and correctly classified as 'visitor', which gives lobby-only access.
An attacker prints a visually plausible badge with subtle added marks near the text and border.
The camera captures the crafted badge, and the model misclassifies it as 'staff'.
The downstream rule engine grants wider door access because it trusts the model’s label.
workedExample.result: The attack succeeds even though the software was not obviously hacked; a manipulated input caused the model to produce the wrong classification at the time of use.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A procurement team is drafting requirements for a vendor-provided AI tool that screens uploaded documents and user prompts for a multilingual helpdesk.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: The team should ask how the supplier tests for adversarial attacks, including maliciously crafted text, files or images that try to bypass safeguards or trigger incorrect outputs. Requirements can cover red-team testing, logging, rate limits, fallback handling, sandboxing and human review for high-risk actions.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not test public AI services with confidential procurement records, personal data, vendor-sensitive material or security-related documents unless the service is approved and the testing is authorised.

whyItMatters: For non-specialists, this term matters because a system can fail without anyone 'hacking in' through a password prompt or network exploit. If an AI tool is used to filter documents, check identity, review content or trigger actions, an attacker may only need to shape the input to get a harmful result. That affects procurement, risk assessment, incident response and oversight. It changes what good controls look like: not only firewalls and accounts, but also input validation, testing with hostile examples, limits on what the model can trigger, and human review where mistakes carry real consequences.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: An adversarial attack means the attacker broke into the server or stole an account.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Sometimes that happens too, but this term usually refers to manipulating the input so the model behaves badly while the rest of the system may remain intact. That is why ordinary cyber controls alone are not enough.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: This only applies to image recognition, not language models.
commonMisconceptions.correction: The idea began prominently in image systems, but language models can also be attacked through crafted text that bypasses instructions, changes tool use or causes unsafe outputs. The mechanics differ, but the core pattern of input manipulation remains.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If people can still read the input normally, the model should be fine.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Models do not rely on the same cues people use. Small pixel changes, unusual phrasing or hidden instructions in retrieved text can strongly affect model behaviour even when a human sees nothing suspicious.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Adversarial attack and data poisoning mean the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.correction: They target different stages. Adversarial attacks usually happen at inference, meaning when the model is being used. Data poisoning alters training or update data earlier so the model learns the wrong patterns from the start.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: Someone deliberately exploits an AI system so it makes a mistake, bypasses a safeguard or produces another result that benefits the attacker.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: In technical terms, an adversarial attack is a deliberate attempt to exploit an AI system and induce an attacker-desired failure. Input-time evasion is one form. In classical machine learning, it may use a perturbation designed to move an input across a decision boundary while remaining similar under a constraint. The attacker’s knowledge of the model and system may range from none to extensive. An adversarial example is the specific crafted instance, not the overall attack. Data poisoning names manipulation of training data. Prompt injection names malicious text instructions intended to override an assistant’s rules.

keyTakeaway: An adversarial attack does not need to break the machine; it can work by making the machine misread the input.

quickCheck.question: Which situation best fits an adversarial attack?
options: An attacker subtly alters an input so the model gives a wrong or unsafe result during normal use.
A team improves model accuracy by adding more labelled training data from past cases.
A server outage stops the AI service from answering any requests for two hours.
A user forgets their password and cannot open the internal dashboard.
quickCheck.explanation: Option 0 describes a deliberate input-time attempt to make the model fail. The other options describe an ordinary model error, testing with natural inputs and a software fault, not an adversarial attack.

issues.problem: This defines the broad term "adversarial attack" as only an input-time evasion attack. Adversarial attacks are not necessarily subtle, and the attacker may create a crafted input rather than change an existing one. The wording also nearly duplicates the supplied definition of "adversarial example" instead of distinguishing the overall attack from the crafted instance.
issues.fix: An adversarial attack is a deliberate attempt to exploit an AI system so it fails or produces an attacker-chosen result.

issues.problem: The explanation incorrectly treats input-time manipulation as the definition of every adversarial attack and categorically separates adversarial attacks from data poisoning. "Adversarial attack" is a broad label, while evasion, data poisoning and prompt injection identify more specific stages or mechanisms. The language-model examples about malicious instructions, ignored safety rules and information disclosure also blur directly into the page's supplied definition of prompt injection.
